steps.premise: Interviews can have titles similar enough to confuse their caption files.
steps.action: Associate each caption file with its interview's catalog number.
steps.consequence: Each recording plays with the words that belong to it.
steps.quote: Match each caption file to the interview's catalog number so two recordings with similar titles don't end up playing with each other's words.

steps.premise: A visitor may have trouble telling voices apart.
steps.action: At each speaker change, show the speaker's agreed name.
steps.consequence: The visitor can tell who said each part of the exchange.
steps.quote: Mark a change of speaker with the name the person agreed to use. A listener who can't distinguish the voices can still follow the exchange.

steps.premise: A sound may explain why the speakers paused or reacted.
steps.action: Briefly describe that sound in the captions when it explains the reaction.
steps.consequence: Visitors can understand what the speakers were responding to.
steps.quote: Include a brief description of a meaningful sound, such as the train whistle both speakers stop to hear, when it helps explain their reaction.

steps.premise: A visitor needs to relate written words to the moment they were spoken.
steps.action: Synchronize each caption with the phrase it represents.
steps.consequence: The displayed words can be followed alongside that phrase in the audio.
steps.quote: Time each caption to the relevant phrase so a visitor can connect the words on screen with the same moment in the recording.

steps.premise: An awkward line break can interrupt a phrase or a person's full name.
steps.action: Break lines where the sentence naturally divides and keep first and last names on one line.
steps.consequence: Visitors can take in each line quickly.
steps.quote: Break lines at natural points in a sentence and keep a person's first and last name together to make the text easier to take in at a glance.

steps.premise: Captions need the correct spellings of names and local landmarks.
steps.action: Have the narrator or a reviewer they nominate check the spellings before display.
steps.consequence: Visitors see spellings that have been checked by someone familiar with the account.
steps.quote: Ask narrators or their nominated reviewers to confirm how people's names and local landmarks are spelled before the captions go on display.

steps.premise: A speaker's characteristic wording can convey part of the story on its own.
steps.action: Keep the narrator's phrasing when writing captions.
steps.consequence: The captions preserve meaning that a polished version might lose.
steps.quote: Keep a narrator's own expressions in the captions. A familiar turn of phrase can carry part of the story that a polished rewrite would lose.

steps.premise: Two reviewers may still be unable to identify a word.
steps.action: Label the word as inaudible in that case.
steps.consequence: Visitors can see where the recording leaves the account unclear.
steps.quote: If two reviewers still can't make out a word, mark it as inaudible so visitors know where the recording leaves a gap in the account.

steps.premise: Visitors need to know what languages they are hearing and which translations they can read.
steps.action: Identify the spoken languages and name each translation on offer.
steps.consequence: Visitors can select the text they want.
steps.quote: Identify which languages are spoken and label each available translation by name so visitors can select the text they want.

steps.premise: Two speakers may be talking at once while both are still understandable.
steps.action: Put the two speakers' words on separate caption lines during the overlap.
steps.consequence: Visitors can see that the remarks happened at the same time.
steps.quote: For overlapping conversation, give the two voices separate lines where both are intelligible. Visitors can see that the remarks were made together.

steps.premise: A visitor may need to find a comfortable text size before a long interview.
steps.action: Give each station a size control and a sample caption on which to try it.
steps.consequence: The visitor can set a suitable size before the interview starts.
steps.quote: Provide a text-size control at each station and let visitors try it on a sample caption before starting a long interview.

steps.premise: An archival image can change from dark to light behind the text.
steps.action: Put captions on a solid background that contrasts with the letters.
steps.consequence: Captions stay readable across changes of image.
steps.quote: Place captions on a solid, high-contrast background so their legibility survives a shift from a dark portrait to a pale archival photograph.

steps.premise: A visitor may want another look at a passage containing several names or dates.
steps.action: Place a replay control where the visitor can readily reach it.
steps.consequence: The visitor can return to that passage and read the details again.
steps.quote: Put a replay control within easy reach for passages with several names or dates that a visitor may want to read again.

steps.premise: A visitor can miss the opening words while looking for caption settings.
steps.action: Make captions visible when a new listening session starts.
steps.consequence: The visitor can read the opening from the start.
steps.quote: Start a fresh listening session with captions visible so a visitor can read the opening words without searching through settings.

steps.premise: Some people want to read an interview on paper and need to identify the right copy.
steps.action: Supply a paper transcript for every recording under the same title used on screen.
steps.consequence: A visitor can pick the printed version of the chosen interview.
steps.quote: Offer a printed transcript for each recording with the same title as the on-screen listing. People who prefer to read on paper can pick the matching copy.

steps.premise: Someone interested in one subject may be listening to a long interview.
steps.action: List the main topics with links to the corresponding moments.
steps.consequence: The listener can go directly to the topic they want.
steps.quote: Give long interviews a short list of topics with jump points, letting someone go straight to the passage about the old school or the flood.

steps.premise: A reply may make little sense when a visitor relies on captions alone.
steps.action: Have a reviewer follow the whole interview with the sound off and flag unexplained replies.
steps.consequence: The review identifies places where the text fails to give the reply enough context.
steps.quote: Ask a reviewer to follow a complete interview with the sound muted and flag places where a reply seems to come out of nowhere.

steps.premise: Cutting a section of the audio can leave its words in the caption track.
steps.action: Check the captions at the cut against the removed passage.
steps.consequence: The review can catch text for words no longer heard.
steps.quote: When an audio edit removes a section, review the accompanying captions for both the missing passage and any timing shift afterward.

steps.premise: Cutting a section of the audio can change the timing of everything that follows.
steps.action: Check the timing of captions after the cut.
steps.consequence: The review can catch later captions that have fallen out of sync.
steps.quote: When an audio edit removes a section, review the accompanying captions for both the missing passage and any timing shift afterward.

steps.premise: Staff need to locate the point where a visitor saw an error.
steps.action: Put fields for the interview title and playback time on the correction slip.
steps.consequence: Staff can find the reported mistake.
steps.quote: Give visitors a correction slip with space for the interview title and playback time so staff can find a reported error.

steps.premise: A narrator may have agreed to public access only with certain information withheld.
steps.action: Check caption text against those restrictions, including names muted in the recording.
steps.consequence: The captions honor the restrictions on the public account.
steps.quote: Check that restrictions agreed with a narrator are reflected in the caption text, including any names that were silenced in the public recording.

steps.premise: Objects near the screen can cover low caption lines from a seated visitor's viewpoint.
steps.action: Inspect the screen from the listening chair.
steps.consequence: The test reveals caption lines hidden from that seat.
steps.quote: Test the screen from the actual listening chair to catch a low caption line that a shelf edge or headphone stand might obscure.

steps.premise: When the narrator reads someone else's letter or diary, a visitor may mistake the quoted words for the narrator's.
steps.action: Use the captions to introduce the excerpt as the narrator begins to read.
steps.consequence: Visitors can identify whose words they are reading.
steps.quote: Introduce a recorded letter or diary excerpt in the captions when a narrator starts reading aloud, so visitors know whose words are being quoted.

steps.premise: A visitor may want an explanation of an unfamiliar custom while following a sentence.
steps.action: Put optional background notes in the interview listing.
steps.consequence: Visitors can look up the custom and keep their place in the narration.
steps.quote: Keep optional background notes in the interview listing. Visitors can look up an unfamiliar local custom without losing their place in the speaker's sentence.

steps.premise: People can arrive partway through a looped interview.
steps.action: Keep its title visible with the captions.
steps.consequence: A visitor who missed the beginning can identify the story in progress.
steps.quote: For an exhibit that plays on a loop, display the interview title alongside the captions so someone arriving midway can place the story.
